---
title: "The agent-based model"
---

## Why agents

A spreadsheet can multiply an assumed penetration rate by a cooling load. Three things
here need agents:

**Heterogeneity that interacts with the physics.** The dwelling that gets hottest belongs
to the household least able to buy cooling. That correlation determines the aggregate, and
it cannot be recovered from city means.

**Peer effects.** Adoption spreads through neighbourhoods. The share of nearby households
already owning an AC enters each decision, so adoption compounds spatially instead of
rising uniformly.

**A feedback loop.** Waste heat raises outdoor temperature, which raises indoor
temperature, which raises discomfort, which raises adoption. The loop only exists if the
agents re-read their environment each year.

## Agents

One household cohort per residential building: an integer count of households, of which an
integer count own an air conditioner. That makes 3.2 million household agents cost two
integer arrays rather than three million Python objects.

| attribute | source |
|---|---|
| households | ward population → residential floor area → archetype occupancy |
| income band | ready-reckoner quartile, slums pinned to the lowest |
| archetype | typology + floor count + slum flag |
| indoor temperature, discomfort | 1R1C model on that building's fabric |
| AC ownership | state variable, updated annually |
| setpoint, runtime | chosen from income band and indoor exceedance |

## The decision

Each year, every household without an AC draws against

$$
u = \beta_0 + \beta_a (\text{afford} - 1) + \beta_d \left(\frac{\text{discomfort}_i}{\text{discomfort}_\text{ref}} - 1\right) + \beta_p\, \text{peer}_i
$$

$$
p_i = \frac{p_\text{cap}}{1 + e^{-u}}
$$

- **afford** rises with real income growth against a falling real AC price, scaled down at
  low income bands (the same price is a larger barrier further down the distribution).
- **discomfort~i~** is that agent's own indoor degree-hours above the comfort threshold,
  including any warming the city has caused itself.
- **peer~i~** is the share of households owning an AC within the agent's neighbourhood,
  computed on a 500 m grid with 3×3 smoothing rather than a radius query — the calculation
  repeats every simulated year over 580,890 buildings.

Adoption is a binomial draw on the non-owning households, so **penetration is an output**.
Nothing forces the trajectory toward a target.

## Operation

Ownership is a weak proxy for heat output: a household cooling one room for two hours a
night and one cooling a whole flat for ten differ fourfold. Two behavioural variables
close that gap.

**Setpoint** falls with income band (27 °C at the bottom, 24 °C at the top).
**Runtime** is logistic in mean indoor exceedance above the setpoint, damped by a bill
sensitivity that is lower for poorer households. Both are read back by the load model.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
ts = pd.read_csv("data/processed/abm2_timeseries.csv")
pd.DataFrame({
  "year": ts.year,
  "penetration %": (100*ts.pen_med).round(1),
  "mean runtime": ts.runtime_med.round(2),
  "Qf mean W/m²": ts.qf_med.round(2),
  "ΔT °C": ts.dt_med.round(2),
  "peak MW": ts.elec_med.round(0).astype(int),
}).set_index("year")
```

The city-wide mean runtime is where the inequality shows up in aggregate: it dropped from
0.74 to 0.60 the moment 284,216 buildings were reclassified as informal, because those
households sit in the highest-setpoint, most bill-sensitive group. Operation behaviour, not
ownership, did that.

## What the model is not

It has no replacement cycle (units are bought, never retired), no explicit tariff slabs, no
tenure split between owners and renters, and no change in the building stock — no
redevelopment, no new construction, no population growth. Commercial and industrial cooling
is a fixed fraction per archetype and sits outside the ABM entirely, despite being 43% of
modelled energy.
